[quote=the_crystalline_empire;61581607][b]On the Economic Issues Facing Re-Unification[/b]
  In the opening note to these papers, President Mjrkanlwyth proposed a bold idea for the potential reunification of Montfleur and Rosenmarkke; however, such a reunification would prove difficult for a variety of reasons. Aside from the clear cultural and political divergences among the regions of the states involved, there is also a significant economic disparity that has arisen in Rosenmarkke and Montfleur. First, financial development has differed greatly in Rosenmarkke than in Montfleur due to Montfleur undergoing the massive decolonisation efforts it had to pursue under the government from 1930 to 1980. Second, Montfleur, under its policy of neutrality, has maintained lower economic inflows from investors and international companies than the more technocratic Rosenmarkke. Third, as a result of the prior two reasons, the financial situation between citizens in Rosenmarkke and in Montfleur has leaned more in favor of Rosenmarkke due to the progressive tendencies of its government in ensuring civilian welfare is maintained at the highest standard, whereas the Montfleurois government has done little, or has been unable to do much, for its own citizens, 18.4% of who, live below the poverty line. 

[i]Financial Development[/i]
As aforementioned, economic development between Rosenmarkke and Montfleur has differed greatly. Whereas Rosenmarkke was able to open itself to the wider market under its semi-socialist welfare system, Montfleur has maintained a relatively closed market for international trade, reluctantly doing trade with the Socialist Internationale. 

As a result, capital inflows for Rosenmarkke are higher, thereby allowing the government of Rosenmarkke to place more emphasis on its welfare system (which is one of the broadest in its region), while also placing a national mandate for economic development via an organised system of private/public economic planning. 

On the opposite side, Montfleur holds a protectionist stance on its economy, which, while holding higher industrial capacity than Rosenmarkke, has failed to reap the benefits of such a large industry, focusing mainly on internal improvements and post-colonial reconstruction. Indeed, it can be argued that the programme of decolonisation, which ran from 1930 to 1980 under those who were called Les Optimistes. Severely damaged Montfleurois development as the government focused primarily on the liberal moral order of decolonisation without focusing on the economic aspects, getting rid of colonies and resources like gifts.

The programme of decolonisation hit Montfleurois industry hard in the late 90s when the state faced a mounting debt crisis on the international stage, failing to pay off the loans that it had taken out to build its industrial capacity to ensure no burden was placed directly upon the citizens, causing a nationwide collapse which saw unemployment and inflation skyrocket and remain at levels that hadnt been perceived until the mid 2010s.   Thus, the ideological basis of governance within Montfleur proved to be its downfall. 

[i]Neutrality[/i]
Another key difference and issue between the two states is the concept of international relations. While one would assume that neutrality would bring in investors and opportunities abroad, this is usually coupled with a government willing and open to permitting such matters to occur. Unfortunately, the government of Montfleur, in its conservativeness, feared that mass investment would ruin the character of the nation, and as a result, limited heavy investment in order to promote a form of autarky. However, once again, the economists and government of Montfleur underestimated the cost of attempted autarky, placing the country back developmentally 10-20 years. 

Whereas Rosenmarkke approached with great eagerness the concept of international relations, seeking to protect itself via trade and economic networks favorable to its government, it was in this plan that the Rosenmarkket economy experienced numerous boom cycles across the late 20th and early 21st centuries, only just now experiencing any significant downturn due to political turmoil. 

It is in this that we can say Rosenmarkke need not unify with Montfleur to stabilise itself; all it needs is to reaffirm to the investors that it can indeed continue and stabilise itself through the pursuit of economic externalism. 

[i]The Financial Situation on the Home Front[/i]

Due to the reasons listed above, the personal financial situation of a citizen in Montfleur versus that of a citizen of Rosenmarkke is a deeply divergent world, whereas the citizen of Rosenmarkke can enjoy high welfare spending and government services, which aid in the tax burden of the state. The citizens of Montfleur struggle to maintain themselves above the poverty line, if not even maintain themselves within the middle class, where the upper echelons of Montfleurois society are locked away due to inheritance, with most industrialist families inheriting properties and companies, thereby creating a hereditary oligarchy in some manner.

Furthermore, the average Rosenmarkket citizen, while suffering from a higher tax burden, enjoys a wider range of freedoms and privileges economically in terms of economic choice; one can go abroad easily, travel across the country in comfort, and move and do business in another region. Whereas the average Montfleurois citizen maintains in their life a limited view of their opportunities, with most not attending university or even secondary education. 

The outdated nature of Montfleurois society further prevents social mobility as prejudices and tensions between the social classes remain, even despite efforts by the left-wing parties in the nation for nearly 200 years to upset the status quo; they have only managed to succeed in popular electoral and political reforms rather than economic ones, primarily due to the moralist majority in the National Assembly of Montfleur. 

[i]Closing[/i]
It is in these reasons that we see major divergences which would prevent or potentially prevent a stable long-term reunification between the two states, whereas the burden of support would fall upon the Rosenmarkke government to maintain and uphold the government of Montfleur and its citizens, thereby potentially risking the economy of Rosenmarkke itself. There simply exist far too many economic divergences in lifestyle, approach, and political nature to justify the lengthy and expansive task of reunifying two nations that have held separate trajectories for centuries now.

  - Josef Alben (Professor of Economics at Vysjllá Technical Institute)[/quote]

[b]The Victory of Reform: Economic Mobilisation and the Working Classes' Roles in Montfleur and Rosenmarkke[/b]

In the letter by the honourable Dr. Josef Alben, various attempts at deriding the unification process and the planning and work of The International Association for the Reunification of Rosenmarkke and Montfleur. While the honourable Dr. Alben did indeed make valid points regarding the divergences between the economies of Rosenmarkke and Montfleur, he failed to note the widespread support in both nations for the workers' parties, which have played a crucial role in the industrial development of both Rosenmarkke and Montfleur. 

[i]The History of Workers' Movements in Rosenmarkke and Montfleur[/i]

The advent of the industrial process in the mid 1700s and early 1800s saw the rise of a great many theories regarding the new class of worker; no longer were the peasant and the tinkerer the primary nodes of economic society, but a third class arose, these being the industrial workers, drawn to the cities and the areas of betterment, they soon became tools in an exploitative system. 

Naturally, these led to mass protests, which shifted the tone of the governments in both Rosenmarkke and Montfleur to accept the new reality that the citizens could indeed rise up and not be easily crushed by the knights and lords of old. As such, Montfleur and Rosenmarkke, seeking to protect the establishment and the state itself, sought to include and reform the systems.

However, while the story remains the same for both Montfleur and Rosenmarkke, the methods of the movements and the adaptation of the states differed greatly.  For instance, in Rosenmarkke, the workers' revolution became a key part of the government, where the government recognized that it was the workers who gave the nation its legitimacy. This is evident in the period known as Red October, which saw thousands of students mobilise against the continuing maintenance of the nobility and the rise of nepotism, even as the state pronounced liberty for all. This was as early as 1839 to 1840 and saw Rosenmarkke become the face of Eastern Elseyran workers' politics for the next century, as successive triumvirates were caught by the ear to listen to the unions and grant them their demands. 

Montfleur, on the other hand, while observing the rise of the liberal order in the 1830s due to the disastrous war against Rosenmarkke in the early 19th century, did not embrace the workers revolution until the 1867 election, which saw the emergence of Li Baptistes within the assembly, as a result of once again student and workers' protests. 

Indeed, to the common socialist, Montfleurois socialism looks cleaner and slower in its process, opting for technological advancement as the primary method by which the bourgeois will become irrelevant. As a result of this, the Montfleurois socialist movement has maintained a steady partnership with its monarchist government, utilizing disgruntlement and political support to move the country leftward. However, as shown in the 1968 protests of Li Montaigne du Berry, the revolution has not been able to overcome the influence of the monarchy, instead being forced to rely on capitalist political and social systems to influence and sway the nation. Indeed, social welfare was not institutionalized until 1987, and a workers' bill of rights was not made until 1969. 

So how then? Given these divergent histories and methods, how then can Rosenmarkket workers and Montfleurois workers come together to form a new nation? The answer comes from Rosenmarkke itself, institutionalizing the revolution in such a manner that it becomes impossible to remove without aggressive and destabilising actions against it.

[i]Implementing the Revolution[/i]

Within both nations, there already exists the core seeds to the furthering of a united peoples movement; it is upon these that unity can be established. Firstly, to foster national unity, a historical common ground must be laid, based upon the present historical facts, where the current systems do not work, and have failed the citizens of both nations. It is in this disgruntlement that we can grow the seed of unity.

Acknowledging the historical facts, we can then turn ourselves towards the common goal, which is the establishment of a united state, governed not by the elite but by the direct hand of the revolution and the people. It is in this common goal that the people (who by far outnumber the government officials) can rise to demand that these limited officials step aside or face the consequences of the public revolution (of which no civil man desires). 

Understanding that most government officials who are not pure ideologues are weak, there is no doubt that the will of the people will be followed for fear of the total destabilisation of both nations, both of which are, as Dr. Alben said, Divergent. It is in this fear of desabilisation that we can produce the feelings and motion of unity, for when a nation is under threat, it naturally rallies around the common movement and the common masses. If such a movement can be created, then unity is most certainly assured.

Already the blocks are in place, the supporters readied at the barricades, now to initiate the charge.

  - Louis Metternisse (Chairman for the department of Ideological Aims of the Montfleurois Socialist Party Li Baptistes)

[quote=lyuongo;61573939][spoiler=Uria]
Petty Officer Thet Mg looked over his map laid across a cheap, plastic table. His defenses were colored chocolate candies spread across the city's perimeter, and the LNSA's formidable offensive brunt a couple of chocolate bars, shaking across the table as artillery fire smashes the city of Uria. He stared at the cheap, makeshift operations room in disgust. Sad. Sad, he thought, how many men will die for some sh*thole place like this. He couldn't believe there was honor dying for a city of concrete rubble of plastic. Men were supposed to die guarding the damsel in distress, massive civilizations of marble and pageantry. Not this. Not this ugly motherf-cking hole in the ground. 

Meanwhile, on the front lines, men shot in the head rolled down the makeshift mound-trenches into the arms of fellow men. Strafing MiGs turned whole groups of men into ground beef prime for taco Tuesday. The few decrepit tanks the LNA dragged from
Naypinau laid the only support artillery for the besieged forces. It was never a question of if, but when the LNSA took the last LNA foothold in the north. For now, however, the LNA held strong. A MiG fired off another missle. Thet Mg flicked another circular chocolate off the map. 

Down south in Ryuloga, President Tung met with officials from the Lyuongoan Mining Corporation. General consensus was that the jungle provided ample defense to keep operating uranium mining operations in the south, and that they needed to use this advantage over the LNSA to vie for foreign support. Further, the LNA must keep its Northern and Southern forces together. What happened at Naypinau and currently at Uria is unacceptable from here on out. The LNA does not have the manpower to waste on entanglements isolated from air support. The LNA would have to figure out a new military doctrine on the fly...

[b]"Set this land ablaze, if one corporation holds its soil when my breath has breathed it last, then I have failed as a man, and as your Marshal."[/b]

Hein orders the Mig bombing runs to begin again even as his own troops are fighting in the streets, he gives assent for the Admiral to open fire, he cracks open boxes of flamethrowers and prepares inferno regiments for the battles to come. He pushes everything he has nearby into this assault, tank drivers push under desperation, and Migs are burning up with their near ceaseless flights and artillery turns orange with the heat of never ending fire. Many of his own are killed in the constant bombing. God willing, it proves fruitful, shock and awe combined with constant assault oughta do it. 

When the inferno divisions are prepared, he splits them off from the main army and sends them with a regiment of jeeps to the rainforests of the north, as close to the uranium fields as they can get without going into a firefight. Then they start the great roasting, including that of native tigerian villages, though Hein does not know of this yet.
